prompt: `val week: List<Int> = listOf(45, 30, 60)` and then `week.add(90)`. What happens?

choices.text: The list grows to four items
choices.why: `List` has no `add` to call.

choices.text: It does not compile: `List` has no `add`
choices.why: Right: `unresolved reference 'add' on receiver of type 'List<Int>'`.

choices.text: It throws `UnsupportedOperationException` when that line runs
choices.why: That is what Java's unmodifiable lists do; Kotlin refuses at compile time.

choices.text: A new list is returned and `week` is unchanged
choices.why: `add` does not exist on `List` at all; `week + 90` would make a new list.

prompt: What does the section recommend a function that builds a list return?

choices.why: That hands every caller a way to change data the function owns.

choices.text: An `Array`, which is cheaper
choices.why: An array can be changed by anybody who holds it.

choices.text: A `Set`, since a set cannot change
choices.why: A `Set` drops repeats, which changes the data; and `MutableSet` changes too.

choices.text: A `List`, built from a private `MutableList`
choices.why: Right: mutable inside, read-only outside.

prompt: `listOf(45, 30, 60, 20).fold(0) { acc, m -> acc + m }`. What is the result?

hint: Where does each get its starting value?

choices.text: `fold` starts from the value you gave it, with no first item needed
choices.why: Right: `reduce` takes the first item, and an empty list has none.

choices.text: `fold` skips empty lists and `reduce` loops forever
choices.why: `reduce` throws at once; it does not loop.

choices.text: `fold` catches exceptions inside the lambda
choices.why: Neither catches anything.

choices.text: `fold` is lazy, so it never reaches the empty part
choices.why: `fold` on a list is eager.
